core: Working definition: the balance sheet is a financial statement that reports what a business owns (assets), owes (liabilities), and is worth to its owners (equity) on a specific date
The shape: the balance sheet is the accounting equation in statement form, assets on one side and liabilities plus equity on the other (equation mechanics owned by sibling topic)
The moment in time: the balance sheet is a snapshot dated 'as of' one day, not a period report
Current vs non-current sections: items expected to be used up, converted, or settled within one year versus beyond one year
Reading the statement: owners look at equity, lenders look at obligations and near-term ability to pay
Balance sheet vs income statement: snapshot of position at a date versus report of performance over a period
Honest framing: the balance sheet always balances by construction; the real question is what the numbers mean
supporting: Statement of financial position as an alternate name for the balance sheet
The balance sheet is one of the three core financial statements (income statement and cash flow statement are sibling topics)
The current/non-current split lets stakeholders see the timing of what must be paid soon versus what can wait
Analysts use balance sheet figures to assess liquidity, financial strength, and leverage, and to calculate ratios (ratio detail owned by sibling topic)
outOfScope: Accounting equation mechanics and double-entry logic (sibling topic accounting-equation)
Detailed asset definitions and types (sibling topic assets)
Detailed liability definitions and types (sibling topic liabilities)
Income statement construction and analysis (sibling topic income-statement)
Statement of cash flows (sibling topic statement-of-cash-flows)
Ratio calculation and interpretation (sibling topic financial-ratios)

claims.claim: A balance sheet is a financial statement that lists what an organization owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and what it is worth (equity) on a specific date.
The balance sheet is a snapshot: it reports financial position at the close of business on a single 'as of' date, not over a period of time.
The balance sheet is the accounting equation in statement form: assets = liabilities + equity, with assets on one side and liabilities plus equity on the other.
The income statement reports financial performance for a given period of time, while the balance sheet reports financial position at a specific date.
Assets are classified as current when they will be used or consumed within one year and non-current when they will serve the business beyond one year.
Liabilities are classified as current when they will be settled within one year and non-current when they are due more than one year out.
The current/non-current split exists because the timing of obligations matters to stakeholders: knowing how much must be paid within a year is more useful than a total alone.
Owners read the balance sheet for equity, the value left for them after liabilities; lenders read it for what the business owes and whether its near-term resources can cover what comes due.
The balance sheet always balances because it is structured around the accounting equation; balancing is a feature of the system, not evidence of financial health.
Analysts use the balance sheet to assess a company's financial strength, liquidity, and capital structure, and to calculate ratios; the real analytical question is what the numbers mean.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the statement called a 'balance sheet' or a 'statement of financial position'?
positions: OpenStax and U.S. practice use 'balance sheet'
CFI notes the statement is 'also called a statement of financial position', the name more common under IFRS
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches 'balance sheet' as the common name and mentions 'statement of financial position' as an alternate name; the two names describe the same statement.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the current/non-current cutoff exactly one year or one operating cycle?
positions: OpenStax 2.2 classifies by whether an item will be used or settled within one year (generally)
CFI defines current as within a year and non-current as beyond a year
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the one-year horizon as the general rule, which both sources state, without teaching the operating-cycle exception in depth.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft described the balance sheet as 'a foundational concept in Accounting' whose purpose is to be 'a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions' — generic boilerplate with no support for what a balance sheet actually is; discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the draft's boilerplate (no definition, no shape, no timing) with the verified snapshot definition, equation-in-statement shape, as-of dating, current/non-current classification, reader perspectives, and by-construction balancing framing.

sourceRecords.title: Balance Sheet: Definition, Template, and Examples
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (page updated December 25, 2025). Supports: the balance sheet as a snapshot of what a company owns (assets), owes (liabilities), and the value left for the owners (shareholders' equity); also called a statement of financial position; structured around the accounting equation assets = liabilities + equity; left side assets, right side liabilities and shareholders' equity; current (within a year) versus non-current (beyond a year) classification of both assets and liabilities; 'the balance sheet must always balance'; use by investors, lenders, and leaders to assess performance, funding needs, and overall financial strength; analyst use for liquidity, efficiency, and leverage assessment and ratio calculation.
